Content:
Have you guys ever break apart an LCD screen say in your old phone and see what that thing is?  When I was in graduate school I was told that thing is liquid crystals, which are these long molecule that can rotate and adsorb light waves,  this way if the wave is parallel to the dipole of this long molecule the polarized light would get adsorbed and so forth.  So I thought I can get these guys out from my busted phone screen and see if I can get them out.  I was told these guys are alighn in an array with all sorts of microscopic electros to make the whole thing produce all the pixels and colors.   But I found not such complicated gagedtry behind these screens.  What I found was this piece of solid black thing withh 5 wires sticking out to be connected to the motherboard.  Assuming one is ground and one is power, this means this thing which is a completely flexible piece of something, requires only 3 signals to produce all the colors and pixels we see.  But not only that, it can even sense our touch with at least two points of contacts, this means at least one wire is a feed back to the OS and the CPU for processing the respone. 

I don't know how this works at all.  All I know is whatever this thing is, it is very similar to the thing. You find behind mirrors.  You can try break one carefully so you don't shatter it by shearing it.  Just cover the whole mirror with a towel, put a small brick in the middle and gently tap it with a wood hammer until it starts cracking and try other areas as needed.  The mirror one is a lot thinner and is clearly just a passive thing but the point is it can't work without the glass, the glass is essential.  It is not your modern glass thought these glasses shatters like the old window glass which you can't find anymore unless you have a really old house.  But anyway they still sale bathroom mirrors so go grab as many as you can before they ban those too like the Obama administration did under the green initiative.   

Now the glass on your iPad is actually not old glass either, it is pyrex if I am right but it can't substitute for the mirror glass.  In fact this particular glass is not even transparent unlike regular pyrex. 

So I have no idea what is going on.  Another thing I discovered while opening up my broken commodore monitor as a kid is that the so call electron cathode ray tube is just a big light bulb and it is totally safe I think just very bright and heavy.  The screen itself is again this material behind the mirror but it was really thick on the TV, maybe they had trouble plaster on because the TV screen is bent to about the same curvature as the light bulb.  I had to open it  because I couldn't see red on that monitor anymore so I thought maybe one of the three cathode ray tube was misfiring or something.  Obviously I had no idea what I was doing so I made sure to only see things from the back.  But when I found no cathode ray tube as pictured in the TV repair manual, I was really puzzled.  I wonder if color TV which was introduced in mid 80s after the Apple 1984 commercial to replace the black and white cathode ray TV is fundamentally different somehow.

By the way the first color TV was built by RCA and based on all our historical documentary, it is clear that everything are black and white prior to 80s.  Reagan was the first color TV president just like JFK was the first TV president 2 decades prior when he declared the Moon Race after supposedly the Russians have already reached it but we have no video records of that fact and the Russians never seem to boast about it either. Author: @thetruthmovement2964
Content:
Yes, there is a fundamental physical limit to magnification, and historically, a significant technical limit was reached as well. The video, "Can you keep zooming in forever?", explores how scientists have pushed past these boundaries to reach the atomic level.
Here's a breakdown of the limits discussed in the video:
1. The Physical Limit: Wavelength
The initial limit to magnification is set by the wavelength of the medium used for imaging:
 * Visible Light: You cannot see objects smaller than the wavelength of light itself. Visible light has a wavelength between 380 and 750 nanometers (NM), while an atom is about 0.1 NM. If the light's wavelength is much bigger than the object, the light will simply diffract or bend around it, making it impossible to resolve the object [00:46].
 * Electron Waves: This limit was bypassed using electron microscopes. Since everything has a wavelike nature (de Broglie hypothesis), electrons can be accelerated to high speeds (around 80% the speed of light) to achieve an extremely short wavelength—around 2 to 3 picometers—offering over 100,000 times more resolution than visible light [01:53].
2. The Technical Limit: Spherical Aberration
Despite using electrons, a new technical barrier was discovered in the form of an unavoidable lens flaw that set a hard limit on the maximum resolution:
 * The Flaw: All radially symmetric lenses (magnetic or glass) suffer from spherical aberration, which causes the edges of the electron beam to focus slightly before the center rays. This results in a blurred focus instead of a single sharp point, and the blurring gets worse the higher the magnification [06:27]. This problem persisted for decades [13:09].
 * The Breakthrough: The hard limit was finally overcome in the late 1990s with the development of the aberration corrector. This device uses a complex system of asymmetric magnets (like hexapoles) to counteract the spherical aberration, allowing scientists to cut the resolution down to only 0.13 NM and achieve a clear focus on individual atoms [17:22].
In summary, modern electron microscopes have now reached the practical limit of resolution, allowing scientists to clearly image individual atoms [20:36].

Author: @firatdurak
Content:
Today I want to ask a question about DNA and causality.

People say: “If the camel didn’t have those features, it couldn’t survive in the desert.”
But I’m not asking about the millions of years of evolution of the camel species.
Adaptation, as you call it, might be a process spanning millions of years. But that’s not my question.

Here is my question:
We have a zygote here. (Inside it: cells, DNA, genes, proteins, atoms, quarks...)
And about 13 months later, this zygote turns into a camel.

Why does combining millions of cells result in a camel?
Why does the gathering of millions of DNA strands result in a human?
Why does the joining of millions of adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine bases give rise to a monkey?
Why does the assembly of millions of atoms produce a horse?
Why does the coming together of millions of quarks turn into a camel—with dense eyelashes and a hump?

These building blocks have no mind, no power, no consciousness... Not even life.
So why do these results arise just because they come together?

What I mean is this:
How does this zygote — that is, these cells, proteins, DNA, genes, atoms, quarks —
turn into a camel that is perfectly suited for the desert, with a hump and long eyelashes?

The answer given is: DNA.
"The specific arrangement of adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine produces this result," they say.

In other words:
"That’s how the code is. That’s how its ancestor’s code was. So it has to be the same."
But that’s not an explanation. That’s a presupposition.

What I’m asking is this:
Why does this result appear in a single individual — in this one zygote?

What we call DNA is just a structure made up of specific sequences of nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon.
But how does the arrangement of these four letters result in all the traits of a camel?

Let’s think in architectural terms:
Imagine we have a blueprint for a mosque with three columns.
Can this blueprint build a mosque by itself? No.
Does it necessitate that the mosque must have three columns? No.

That mosque only takes shape if someone with knowledge, will, and power builds it according to the plan.

DNA is the same. It may be a plan.
But that plan alone cannot give rise to a living being with dense eyelashes and a hump.

If we compare the relation between DNA and appearance to the mosque example:
When we look at the blueprint, we can say, “Ah, look, it has three columns.”
But when we look at DNA, we can’t say, “Ah, the eyelashes are thick, the hump is big.”

So how does a code made up only of nitrogen, carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms
result in a camel suited for desert life at the end of a 13-month process?

They give the mutation example:
"If adenine mutates, the eyelashes don’t come out thick," they say.
But even that isn’t an explanation. That still doesn’t prove causality. It’s just correlation.

At this point, I want to recall al-Ghazali’s example of the donkeys:
Every day, the first donkey is ridden, and then the second one.
An observer may assume: “The second donkey moves only after the first one does.”
But this is just a habitual sequence. This is not causality.

A similar claim is made between DNA sequences and phenotype (appearance):
"If this DNA sequence is present, this appearance results."
But this is merely repeated correlation — not necessary causation.

Now look at matter at its deepest level:

Look at the nucleotide sequences in DNA.
Look at the proteins they form.
Then at the atoms that make up those proteins (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen...).
And go even deeper — down to quarks...

None of them has intelligence, will, power, or consciousness.
So how do these arrangements result in a camel, with a hump and eyelashes, adapted for the desert?

How do these materials know that the eyelashes need to be thick?
How do they know there will be wind, sun, or drought?

This is where adaptation narratives come in:
First, they want you to believe the code determines everything.
Then they talk about selection processes that span millions of years:
"Those with fewer eyelashes were eliminated; those with more eyelashes survived."

But that first assumption — that a camel necessarily comes out of the code — is never explained.
And all explanations are built on that assumption.

This leads us to one conclusion:
Now you no longer feel the need for a Creator or a source of power.
You no longer feel the need to seek mercy, will, or knowledge.
Because you act as if DNA does everything.

But in truth, this is a veiling of the evidence — a suppression of signs.

In the end, everything is made up of elements:
Nitrogen, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen...
No one can explain why these elements become a camel, a human, or a monkey.

Causality is always based on repeated patterns and outcomes.
But that’s only correlation.

That is a belief.

And that’s what I’m questioning.
It’s like always writing the letter “K” with a red pen, and the letter “M” with a blue pen.
Then saying, “The letter M must be written with a blue pen.”
But no! The blue pen does not produce the letter M.
We’re just observing a familiar pattern.

Likewise, DNA does not produce that trait.
We’re merely naming a familiar pattern.

But such a pattern requires a “pen-holder.”
It requires a being with will, knowledge, and power.

This is what I’m trying to say.
Trying to tell millions of years of stories without asking this question
is actually an attempt to cover up the real issue.

Author: @vansf3433
Content:
No human eye or optical camera can see an atom. Atoms are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light, so light itself can’t resolve them.

Tools like STM, AFM, or TEM detect effects — tiny currents, force changes, scattered electrons — and feed those numbers into a computer.

The computer turns those numbers into a picture of bright and dark dots.

Humans interpret each dot as an “atom,” but it’s an indirect representation, not the atom’s “appearance.”

 it’s a visualisation (a human-created representation), not a literal view. It’s very much like a mirage , but what you see on the screen is a human interpretation, not atoms themselves. It is an illusion of atomic structure rather than a direct “photograph” of atoms themselves.

Author: @JamesHoch7
Content:
When you “zoom in” on something—say, a photo, a map, or even the physical world—there’s always a limit:

Digital zoom (images/screens): Limited by the resolution of the file. Once you’ve used up all the pixels, further zooming just enlarges blur.

Microscopes/telescopes: Limited by physics. Optical microscopes can only resolve details down to about 200 nanometers (due to the wavelength of visible light). Electron microscopes go much deeper, but eventually quantum effects and noise set a hard floor.

Mathematics (fractals): On paper, fractals like the Mandelbrot set let you “zoom forever” because they’re defined by math, not physical limits. In practice, though, computers hit limitations (processing power, memory, precision of numbers).

Physical universe: Matter itself has a bottom—atoms, then subatomic particles, then down to scales like quarks and the Planck length (~1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m). Below that, physics as we know it doesn’t let you zoom further; space itself may not even have a meaningful “smaller.”

So: in math, kind of yes. In the real world, no—there’s always a limit.

Author: @alienteknology5390
Content:
Once you get down to spotting a single atom, you are just seeing the electron probability cloud because of the Heisenberg Principle. You can't nail a sub atomic particle's exact position in time & space. So it's just a fuzz. If, with sufficient advancements, we are able to get past this, then we could possibly magnify down to the quarks which make up protons & neutrons. Beyond that is anyone's guess. If, with even more advancements, we were to discover that quarks have components as well, then there would be more revelations. Beyond that, according to the standard model, we can only magnify down to the Planck distance, (the smallest possible distance.)
   I am not a physicist. I'm not even a science fiction writer! But this is what i understand to date.

To be fair, I had undiagnosed ADHD, and often skimmed the text books, or retained very little due to distractions. They probably explained much of this, and I just didn't retain details enough to comprehend the function of an electron microscope. But hearing the explanation, and seeing the visuals here has really helped me understand.

Great video.

Author: @azniscannedrice
Content:
You can do something even crazier with STEMs called electron ptychography that allows you to generate/construct images in a manner very loosely similar to how bats use echolocation (sound waves) to "see" their prey. As we all know, electrons can behave like waves. So when a bunch of electrons in a beam are shot at solid samples in an STEM microscope, they produce multiple diffraction patterns each translated some distance with respect to one another (because the electron beam is scanning the sample). And then, through a series of complicated fourier transforms, you can use this dataset of diffraction patterns to back-calculate the original structure of your sample. And because you're calculating the image rather than directly capturing it with detectors, it avoids all lens-induced aberrations, yielding a significant improvement in resolution over conventioal lens based imaging. This allows for some pretty crazy stuff, like "seeing" individual electron orbitals in heavy element atoms. 

Insane.

Author: @rogierownage
Content:
How can you actually see atoms at only 50 million times enhancement? The amount of atoms needed for a reasonable amount of grams of something, is in the order of magnitude of ~10^23. That's astronomically more than 50 million.

Edit: I guess it's a similar principle to the square-cube law. The microscope enhances at a linear scale, so you could effectively imagine that you're putting the enhancement factor to the third power (which doesn't really make sense for a microscope because the image has 2 dimensions). But if you imagined doing it anyways, 50 million times enhancement would be equivalent to ~10^23 which is my earlier estimation, exactly.

There is still space between the atoms and stuff, but it probably lies close to that order of magnitude, so it makes sense.

Author: @BrockLewis-n7m
Content:
🎯 Key points for quick navigation:

00:00 *🔍 Atoms visualized: The video discusses visualizing atoms at extreme magnifications, a feat deemed impossible 30 years ago.*
00:29 *💡 Why atoms are hard to see: Atoms can't be seen with visible light due to their size, requiring alternative methods like electron microscopy.*
01:26 *⚛️ De Broglie's discovery: Everything, even matter, exhibits wavelike properties, culminating in advancements like electron microscopy.*
01:56 *📏 Electron wavelength: The wavelength of electrons in electron microscopy is incredibly small, enhancing resolution dramatically.*
02:25 *🔬 Focusing electrons: The challenge of focusing electrons led to innovations like electromagnetic lenses in electron microscopes.*
03:48 *🧪 First electron microscope: Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll developed the first electron microscope, achieving significant magnification.*
05:11 *🏗️ Overcoming limitations: Despite challenges like spherical aberration, scientists like Ruska improved electron microscope magnification.*
06:12 *🎯 Spherical aberration issue: Spherical aberration in lenses posed a significant barrier to improving electron microscopy resolution.*
06:40 *🔍 Correcting aberrations: Using diverging lenses counteracts spherical aberration but is not feasible with magnetic lenses.*
08:03 *🧲 Magnetic lens challenge: The inability to create diverging magnetic lenses hindered progress in electron microscopy.*
09:00 *🏆 Field ion microscope: The field ion microscope captured the first image of atoms, marking a milestone before electron microscopes caught up.*
10:25 *🛡️ Data privacy concern: A brief promotion for Incogni highlights data privacy, tying into the research process.*
11:23 *🌟 Crewe's innovation: Albert Crewe's directed electron source led to brighter images in the transmission electron microscope.*
12:43 *🖼️ Atomic imaging breakthrough: Crewe's advancements resulted in the first images of single atoms using electron microscopy.*
14:09 *🌀 Non-symmetric lenses: Breaking lens symmetry offered a potential solution to bypass spherical aberration limitations.*
15:04 *🔄 Lens distortion technique: Using hexapole magnets, scientists managed to partially correct spherical aberration in microscopes.*
17:22 *📸 Perfected imaging: Urban, Rose, and Haider achieved clear atomic images by successfully counteracting spherical aberration.*
20:13 *🏅 Award-winning innovation: The breakthrough in correcting spherical aberration earned key figures in microscopy the Kavli Prize.*
20:39 *⚙️ Impact on research: Correcting aberrations is crucial for material sciences, enabling detailed study at the atomic level.*

Author: @Theorist_knowledge
Content: If we zoom into a metal and keep going deeper into its atoms, we first find protons, neutrons, and electrons. But if we zoom in even more, we discover that protons and neutrons are made up of even smaller particles called quarks. These quarks are held together by the strong force. Going further, we reach fundamental particles, like quarks, leptons (like electrons), and bosons that mediate forces. At this level, we’re entering the mysterious world of quantum physics, where particles can behave in strange and unexpected ways, like existing in multiple places at once or being “entangled” with each other.

Author: @wolpumba4099
Content:
*Title: The Incredible Difficulty of Seeing Atoms*

*   *0:00:00** Introduction to Atomic Scale:* The video begins by emphasizing the incredibly small size of atoms, zooming in by factors of thousands and millions to reveal individual atoms.
*   *0:00:41** Why Seeing Atoms is Hard:* Visible light, with wavelengths between 380 and 750 nanometers, is much larger than atoms (around 0.1 nanometers), making it impossible to image them directly.
*	*0:01:06** Solution, smaller wavelengths:* To resolve something you must use something that is much smaller in wavelength.
*   *0:01:11** Electrons as a Solution:* Electrons, due to their wave-like nature (as described by de Broglie's hypothesis), have much smaller wavelengths than visible light, especially when accelerated to high velocities.
*   *0:01:39** Relativistic Electrons:* At 300 kilovolts, electrons reach relativistic speeds (around 80% the speed of light) and have wavelengths of about 2-3 picometers.
*   *0:02:21** Focusing Electrons:* Unlike light, electrons cannot be focused using glass lenses. Ernst Ruska developed electromagnetic lenses by coiling wire and passing a current through it, creating a magnetic field that focuses the electron beam.
*   *0:03:15** Lorentz Force:* The magnetic field in the electromagnetic lens exerts a Lorentz force on the electrons, causing them to spiral and converge towards the center.
*   *0:03:54** First Electron Microscope:* Ruska and Max Knoll built the first transmission electron microscope (TEM) using this electromagnetic lens design.
*   *0:04:10** Image Formation in TEM:* The focused electron beam passes through a very thin sample (around 100 nanometers thick). Electrons are scattered differently by different parts of the sample, creating an "electron imprint."
*   *0:04:46** Ruska's Improvement:* Ruska continued to improve the TEM, achieving magnifications beyond 10,000x, surpassing optical microscopes in imaging capabilities.
*   *0:05:11** Scherzer's Theorem:* Otto Scherzer identified a fundamental limitation: spherical aberration in radially symmetric magnetic lenses, which distorts the image and limits resolution.
*   *0:06:44** Spherical Aberration in Optical Lenses:* Even optical lenses suffer from spherical aberration, but it can be minimized by adding a diverging lens to counteract the converging lens.
*   *0:07:29** Impossibility of a Diverging Magnetic Lens:* Due to the nature of magnetism (North and South poles always coexisting), it's impossible to create a radially symmetric magnetic lens that diverges electrons, as per Maxwell's equations.
*	*0:08:30** Stoppage of progress:* Because of the impossibility to create a diverging magnetic lense, progress of TEM stops.
*   *0:08:55** Alternative Atomic Imaging:* The field ion microscope (FIM) achieved the first generally accepted images of atoms, but it was limited to imaging the surface of a sharp needle tip.
*   *0:11:06** Continued TEM Development:* Despite limitations, work on TEM continued, with Albert Crewe developing a scanning TEM (STEM) using a more directed electron source and a scanning method inspired by cathode ray tube TVs.
*   *0:12:43** First Atomic Images with STEM:* Crewe successfully captured images of individual atoms using his STEM in 1970.
*   *0:13:25** Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM):* The invention of the STM provided another way to image atoms, relying on quantum tunneling effects rather than lenses, thus avoiding spherical aberration.
*   *0:14:04** Breaking Symmetry:* A key insight was that breaking the radial symmetry of the magnetic lens could potentially overcome Scherzer's theorem.
*   *0:14:26** The "Troublemakers":* Knut Urban, Max Haider, and Harold Rose, despite being considered "troublemakers" and facing funding challenges, pursued this unconventional approach.
*   *0:14:46** Non-Symmetric Lens Design:* Their idea was to use a series of non-symmetric electromagnets (hexapoles, octopoles, decapoles) to create a slightly diverging region within the lens to correct for spherical aberration.
*   *0:16:50** Initial Failure and Persistence:* Their first attempt failed, but after 24 hours of stabilization, the new lens produced clear images of atoms, achieving the "impossible."
*   *0:17:25** Improved TEM Resolution:* This breakthrough reduced the resolution limit of the TEM to 0.13 nanometers, dramatically improving image quality.
*   *0:17:40** Initial Skepticism and Eventual Recognition:* The group's initial presentation was poorly attended, but word of their achievement spread, leading to widespread acclaim.
* *0:18:18** sample setting:* Shows the small sample on the tip of the sample holder.
*	*0:19:08** Aligning the sample:* Properly aligned to view atoms "like pearls on a string".
*   *0:20:07** Independent Achievement and Awards:* Ondrej Krivanek independently achieved aberration correction in the STEM, and the groups were awarded the prestigious Kavli Prize.
*   *0:20:27** Routine Atomic Imaging:* Today, imaging atoms with aberration-corrected TEM and STEM is commonplace.
*   *0:20:36** Impact of Aberration Correction:* Aberration correction has revolutionized materials science, chemical engineering, and other fields by enabling detailed atomic-level analysis and understanding of materials' properties.

The concept of "zooming in" on a physical object is indeed lunacy.

From a technical perspective, zooming in on a physical object would require a physical mechanism to reduce the distance between the observer and the object. However, as you continue to zoom in, you'd eventually reach the physical limits of the object itself.

At the molecular level, the object's surface would become increasingly irregular, with atoms and molecules arranged in a complex, three-dimensional structure. Attempting to zoom in further would require penetrating the object's surface, which is impossible without causing physical damage or destruction.

Furthermore, even if it were possible to somehow magically zoom in on an object without physical constraints, you'd eventually reach the quantum level, where the principles of wave-particle duality and uncertainty would render the concept of "zooming in" meaningless.

In short, attempting to zoom in on a physical object is a lunatic endeavor, as it defies the fundamental laws of physics and the nature of reality itself.

Author: @bythelee
Content:
It almost seems too convenient that an atom (or rather, column of atoms) appears as a neat sphere. 
Bearing in mind the atom is a tiny nucleus surrounded by an orbiting cloud of even tinier electrons (I think of planets orbiting our sun as a scale reference), the notion that these appear as a "solid" sphere (of presumably the outermost electron orbit shell) seems so completely wrong. But perhaps this is why the COLUMN is important. Stack enough atoms on top of each other, and the total number of electrons in the clouds becomes like a solid lump of electrons. Or maybe it's the speed? Electrons moving so fast, they appear to be everywhere in their orbit at once? 

VERY cool to see the perfect crystal lattice of the atoms bonded together to make the solid. No gaps, no holes, no inclusions (foreign atomic substance) not even any straining (variation in atomic spacing). I now wonder what vibration (amplitude and frequency) the atoms are shaking at. Because only at absolute zero does that lattice lack any energy to vibrate at all. Is that the next target for atomic microscopy?

Suddenly it doesn't seem so alien that something as sparsely distributed as an atom can seem "solid", such that nothing (like your hand) can pass through it. 

I have dreamed of seeing this image for nearly 50 years, imagining what the structure might look like at the atomic scale after reading about atoms and nuclear structure in a big "Junior book of Science" back in the 1970's.
Thank you Veritasium for fulfilling one of my bucket list items. 


PS I am always stunned and impressed when a native foreign language speaker (I suspect German in this case, from the accent) can speak such flawless, and such TECHNICAL, language. 
Us English speakers have it far too easy, not needing to operate on this kind of subject matter in a second language. 
Could anyone read any of those German technical papers? No? Shame on you...

Author: @BoobaPog
Content: My father operates a lab that specializes in cellular research by using electron microscopes to captures incredibly detailed images of the interior of cells, which help scientists understand cellular functions by examining their internal architecture. The process is super interesting and it begins with isolating a single cell that has been cryogenically frozen, this single cell  will serve as the sample. Once the sample is prepared, it is placed into the Electron microscope. Then a powerful laser pulse focused into the shaped of a line measuring just a few atoms in width will with mind blowing precision perfectly splits the frozen cell into two equal halves. After the cell has been cut, the electron microscope can capture these stunning cross-section images of the cell, where we can see these super complex internal structures of the cell.

Author: @mathis8210
Content:
17:40 - I think you are overdoing this "poor downtrodden ignored scientists" trope. People outside the scientific community will get a very wrong image of how the scientific community functions. They were not ignored over some kind of malice or arrogance. 

From my experience novel projects are welcome and people like to keep an eye on them as they proceed. And there are usually very good reasons to criticise them. Those are the very real  problems with their approach that need to be solved before it becomes viable. Many projects never actually solve these issues and get abandoned at some point.

This is a feature of the scietific method, not a bug. When they did not produce results, they were relegated to a smaller venue for those with specific interest in their detailed progress.
Once they actually produced a result, they immediately got the full attention of the broader community. This is a system of MERIT.
You cant get acknowledged for a discovery before you make said discovery!

Author: @TWENTYSEVENREC
Content:
Are we living in a simulation? The more we dive into the fundamental building blocks of matter—everything from living organisms to everyday objects and even the trees in nature—the more it feels like we’re staring at the "code" that makes up our reality. It’s like we’re in the ultimate cheat code, but with no way to turn it off. Think about it: we’re looking at atoms—the tiny building blocks of everything around us—and they seem to follow a set of rules. Kind of like how video game characters never randomly fall through the floor (unless you’re playing a buggy game... don’t get me started on that). It’s as if there’s a hidden manual that tells everything how to behave, and no one lost it. It’s almost like the universe is programmed with instructions.

Sound familiar? It should. It’s just like a video game, where the world is made up of "bits"—except these "bits" are atoms, and instead of avatars, they form trees, mountains, and maybe even your snack. It’s like if we all had our own NPCs, and they're just trying to do their thing without getting glitched. These particles seem to know exactly how to interact and prevent things from falling apart. Now imagine if the code was written so well that things never fell through the floor, even if you're not paying attention. No bugs, no crashing. Just smooth sailing... or, well, smooth atoms.

But wait—here’s where it gets wild. The oddity goes deeper when you look at quantum mechanics. You’ve probably heard of the Double Slit Experiment, right? If not, picture this: particles behaving like waves until someone looks at them—then, BAM! They act like particles again. It’s like that one friend who only starts doing their homework when the teacher walks by. Where was that focus five minutes ago? The crazy part? The particles seem to only "render" when we're watching, like a video game where the NPCs only appear when you’re near them. Could we be living in some kind of simulation, where the universe is just waiting for us to "log in" to do anything?

We could also entertain the idea that this universe was designed by a divine genius, an all-knowing mastermind who programmed everything down to the last atom. Either way, it’s a pretty mind-blowing thought. We’re like tiny ants in the world’s most advanced video game. But instead of collecting coins, we’re trying to understand why our coffee cup never spontaneously explodes... yet.

But wait, there’s more! Even sound waves create patterns—seriously! You think music is just for dancing, but those sound waves are actually out here forming symmetrical, mathematical patterns like the universe’s version of a DJ. It’s like nature’s playlist always following some cosmic beat. If you step outside and really observe, you’ll see that even the smallest objects in nature follow precise patterns—like the spiral of a seashell or the branching of a tree. Nature’s really out here like, “Check out these fractals! Bet you didn’t expect that.”

The bottom line? Everything in the universe—whether it’s a tree, a rock, or even the atoms that make up your coffee cup—seems to be part of some larger, intricate design. Whether it's physics, sound, geometry, or mathematics, there’s a whole lot of code running the show. Seriously, it’s like the universe is one big program, and we’re all just players trying to figure out if the game is about to crash or if we’re about to unlock some new level of understanding. But what’s wild is that we might not even know we’re in the simulation… until we hit "ctrl+alt+del" and everything resets.

At the end of the day, it feels like the universe is following some kind of calculation, some grand cosmic code. So the next time you’re staring at your phone screen, just remember: your coffee cup might just be doing a little math in the background too.

This raises interesting questions about how the Big Bang's earliest moments could be represented in such a system.

### **The Planck Length as a "Pixel" in a Simulated Universe**
In many simulation-based hypotheses, reality is often described as **discrete** rather than continuous. If the universe were a computational simulation, the **Planck length (\(\ell_P \approx 1.616 \times 10^{-35}\) m)** might correspond to the smallest possible "step" in spatial resolution.

1. **The Smallest Object at the Big Bang?**
   - The earliest state of the universe, near the **Planck time** (\(t_P \approx 5.39 \times 10^{-44}\) s), was dominated by quantum gravitational effects.
   - If the universe was pixelated at the Planck scale, the **smallest possible object** would be a **single "Planck unit" of space**—essentially a **Planck-length-sized "pixel" of space-time**.
   - This could correspond to a **quantum of space**, possibly something like a loop in **loop quantum gravity** or a unit of space-time foam.

2. **How Many Pixels in the Observable Universe?**
   - The observable universe has a radius of ~\(10^{26}\) meters.
   - Dividing by the Planck length gives:
     \[
     \frac{10^{26} \text{ m}}{10^{-35} \text{ m}} \approx 10^{61}
     \]

### **Conclusion: Is the Planck Length a Pixel?**

- The **first meaningful "object" in the Big Bang** would be a single Planck-scale unit of space-time, possibly carrying a minimal amount of **information, energy, or curvature**.

Author: @TheJonesMcCoy
Content:
I asked ChatGPT "is it possible to have a planck lenght magnet" I got a nice answer as follows: A magnet the size of a Planck length (\(1.616 \times 10^{-35}\) meters) is physically implausible for several reasons:

### 1. **Quantum Gravity and the Planck Scale**
   - The Planck length is the scale at which quantum gravitational effects become significant. At this scale, space-time is expected to be highly fluctuating ("foamy"), making it unclear whether classical concepts like "a magnet" can even exist.

### 2. **Magnetism and Particle Size**
   - Magnets arise from moving electric charges or intrinsic spin (as in electrons). The smallest known magnetic moments are those of elementary particles, such as the electron, which has a magnetic moment due to its intrinsic spin. However, an electron itself is vastly larger than the Planck length when considering its Compton wavelength (~\(2.4 \times 10^{-12}\) m).
   - Even if you somehow tried to make a single atom or particle into a "magnet" at the Planck scale, the uncertainty principle ensures that its position and momentum are not well-defined.

### 3. **Domain Size and Magnetic Materials**
   - In classical materials, magnetism typically comes from aligned atomic dipoles within magnetic domains. These domains are many orders of magnitude larger than the Planck scale (~\(10^{-9}\) m and larger).

### 4. **Physical Meaning of a Magnet at the Planck Scale**
   - If you tried to confine a system to the Planck length, quantum fluctuations would dominate, and the concept of a stable dipole or magnetic field wouldn't make sense in the usual way. The energy required to localize a particle within a Planck-scale region would be so high that it could collapse into a black hole.

### **Conclusion**
A "Planck-length magnet" is not possible in any conventional sense because:
   - The physical concepts of magnetism, material structure, and even stable space-time break down at the Planck scale.
   - Quantum gravity and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle prevent anything from being meaningfully localized to that scale.
   - The fundamental magnetic moments (such as electron spin) are already associated with much larger length scales.

If we ever develop a theory of quantum gravity that meaningfully describes physics at the Planck scale, it might redefine how we think about magnetic fields, but in today's physics, the idea is not feasible.

Content:
At what spacial resolution/magnification do you have to start worrying about temporal resolution? (I don't know the actual terms)

Everything above 0K is wiggling about to some degree, that movement means that at one moment, they are in one position and the next, another. On the macro scale, that can be seen as motion blur, but with a fast enough camera, you can remove that blur.

But on the atomic scale, where everything is jiggling about to varying degrees, surely as you zoom in, things are going to look more and more fuzzy due to this motion.

What happens when we start zooming down to the planck scale (and beyond?) How do we get clear images without cooling everything down to 0K?

Author: @eltiess
Content: Correction: field ion microscopes do not have helium shooting at a sharpened tip. I mean, generally it isn't just helium that you can use. But these gas atoms are thermally accommodated on the cryo-cooled tip (30-60K). These gas atoms migrate toward the tip's sharp end where the field is strongest and are ionised when they enter a zone which is at a critical distance above the surface. The field at this critical distance has structure which often demonstrate atomic structures and so you can get a good atomically-resolved FIM micrograph.

Author: @Cardifyz
Content: At 4:10, there is a slight misconception. Contrast in TEM is not solely due to thickness; rather, it primarily arises from diffraction effects. Electrons that are closer to satisfying the Bragg condition diffract more strongly, leading to darker regions in the image. Additionally, we do not "see atoms" directly; instead, atomic-resolution imaging in TEM relies on phase contrast in conventional TEM or Z-contrast in scanning TEM (STEM). In high-angle annular dark field (HAADF) STEM imaging, contrast is generated by Rutherford scattering, where heavier elements (higher atomic number, Z) scatter electrons more strongly, producing brighter regions. For example, in SrTiO3, the Sr and Ti columns appear brighter than the oxygen columns due to their higher atomic numbers. This is one of the best videos on youtube talking about TEM and STEM modes and how they can be used for scientific studies!

Author: @mikmop
Content:
If I were to speculate: "how will this technology continue to evolve over time", then I would say...

...with current TEMs (transmission electron microscopes), we've already imaged individual atoms under carefully controlled conditions, but this is only the beginning.

As this technology continues to improve, we'll probably be able to push the resolution even further and eventually get into the realm of mapping electron orbitals, or even subtle quantum effects around the atoms.

So the next revolution might be in the realm of hybrid instruments that can combine multiple imaging methods, electrons, ions and X-rays. This fusion could offer both high resolution and material-specific information (like chemical composition).

Another revolution could be in the realm of real-time, dynamic imaging. With in-sutu experiments, electron microscopy could eventually allow real-time observation of processes like chemical reactions, crystal growth, or biological processes at the nanoscale. This “in situ” or “operando” approach would allow us to watch changes as they happen, rather than just viewing static snapshots.

Other developments could involve lower damage and more gentle methods. Further progress in low-voltage electron beams or alternative techniques (e.g., cryo-EM for biological samples) could help preserve delicate structures, enabling the ability to watch living or near-living materials with minimal damage.

Smarter automation & AI integration could allow automated analysis. As images get more complex, AI and machine learning will play a bigger role in interpreting data and will be able to spot anomalies, identifying patterns, and classifying structures at scale.

Faster workflows will allow automated microscopes that can self-calibrate and by self-focusing, this could make high-throughput nanoscale imaging more accessible. We then might be able to run vast batches of samples with minimal human input.

There could be an increasing number of applications in materials and medicine, which lead us to new discoveries in material design. By visualizing and manipulating structures at atomic levels, we could engineer new materials with bespoke properties (e.g., superconductors, ultra-strong or ultra-light materials).

Targeted drug delivery and nanomedicine could become more common with electron microscopy, as it helps refine nano-carriers for medications, aiding in targeted therapy research. Detailed 3D imaging of cells and viruses could guide the design of more precise treatments.

It might even push our understanding of fundamental science and quantum boundaries. Techniques that push resolution beyond typical “practical” boundaries might offer glimpses into quantum-scale phenomena that lie between classic physics and quantum mechanics.

As we get better at imaging the invisible, we might evolve additional interdisciplinary connections and find overlaps with other advanced fields like quantum computing, photonics, and nanoelectronics, spurring cross-pollination of ideas.

Overall, the future of high-resolution microscopy involves not just seeing smaller things, but being able to interact with them in ways that lead to transformative science and technology.

From discovering new materials to creating breakthroughs in biology and medicine, ongoing progress in electron microscopy and related fields could reshape how we explore and manipulate the very fabric of our world and completely transform the societies we live in.

Content:

Content:
I was just looking at options the other day on how to see an atom with my own eye as an ordinary everyday person. And apparently there are two options according to the hard research I did (i.e. using Perplexity):
1) Technorama Science Centre, Switzerland
Visitors can observe strings of barium ions fluorescing under laser light using a linear Paul trap. Pushing a button triggers transitions between bright/dark states, making individual atoms visible through an eyepiece. This is one of the few places where the public can directly view single atoms in real time.
2) University Open Days
Labs with scanning tunneling microscopes (STMs) or transmission electron microscopes (TEMs) occasionally host public demonstrations. For example, Cornell University’s STM research has produced atomic-resolution images.

Author: @joshuahancock2079
Content: 4:20  Yes and no. The electrons aren’t being absorbed into the sample at the thicker points. Instead they are being scattered more intensely at the thicker (or denser) points. So these scattered electrons don’t line up in the image at the end, leaving dark spots where they were scattered away from. An aperture can even be added to completely filter off these scattered electrons to increase contrast. This is called “bright field”, and is a technique also used in optical microscopes. Some electrons are absorbed by the sample, but much too few to see contrast. That is from the scattering, not the absorption.

Author: @-BuddyGuy
Content: I worked on ellipsometers in semiconductors and they were more precise than the TEM for measuring dimensions. Unbelievably precise when you had a state of the art one pushed to its limits. The numbers achieved in industry are insane and constantly moving forward. The difference was mostly down to the effects of sample preparation for the TEM I think. The ellipsometer has very specific usage limitations and is measuring averages across a field (sort of) and the TEM is used for making out irregular detail, obviously in that respect the TEM is vastly superior. The coolest technology I saw used a sort of ultrasound to measure metal thickness with a pulsed laser creating strain pulses with thermal expansion. A split beam with a delay from the same source measured the surface reflectivity change over picoseconds (strain influenced the reflectivity). The very thinnest metals were so thin they were transparent, so you could use an ellipsometer on them instead. But the laser doodad was cooler.

Author: @michaelscott466
Content: It’s a bit disingenuous to claim that you're actually "seeing" individual atoms when, in reality, what we're looking at is a representation based on electron density and scattering patterns. Atoms themselves are far too small to be photographed directly. What high-resolution electron microscopes are capturing are not the atoms themselves but rather the way electrons interact with them, providing an indirect image of their position and structure. These are more like inferred maps of atomic arrangements rather than true snapshots of the atoms.

Now a video about focused ion beam (FIB) instrument - the amazing tool that produced this TEM sample - would be a nice! The FIB is also an engineering marvel and the advances it made for sample preparation for TEM is also a large reason the field has grown so fast.

Content: I was in grad school in the 90's and designed and built STMs (scanning tunneling microscope) from scratch. Heinrich Roher(Nobel for STM) would visit our lab and on occasions took 'images' obtained with my microscope and show it during his public presentations. On my return to my grad-school, nearly two decades later, I was so pleased to see those microscopes I built as a grad student were still in use !  (Normally equipment tend to become obsolete quickly) We were a handful of people after Rohrer and Binnig to come up with our own designs of commercially viable STMs (and later spun out companies manufacturing them and other like AFM, scanning near-field optical microscopes, etc ). I still remember those graduate school days when one could 'see' atoms with equipment one built from scratch. It was wonderful. It is nice to see how science keeps progressing

Author: @e.d.8924
Content:
If you look at the expression for wave length you'll see that the wave length is proportional to the reciprocal of the mass.
One may thus ask: "why not use an object with larger mass like a tennis ball and this way get an even smaller wave length"
Well the thing is that a tennis ball have many particles in it so it has a huge thermal noise and in addition to that a tennis ball will interact with the sample (and other objects outside the sample) as a whole so it is useless in that regard.
*But* it is true that using protons instead of electrons will give a better resolution even without accelerating them to 80% of the speed of light.
Using molecules might be even better although in the case of molecules one needs to consider their rotation and vibration modes which can interfere with the scanning.
The usage of electron instead of protons is mainly because it us much easier to create a source of free electrons than a siurce of free protons.
A source of free ions is also possible but than again one needs to take into account the electronic internel degrees of freedom of the ions.

Author: @raphaelgarcia9576
Content:
Always fun to learn about Theorized Improvements:
	•	Shorter Wavelengths: Using X-ray microscopy or gamma-ray microscopy could theoretically achieve even higher resolution since these wavelengths are much smaller than visible light or electrons. However, challenges with lens materials and interactions with matter make this difficult.
	•	Quantum Microscopy: Exploiting quantum entanglement and squeezed light could bypass diffraction limits and improve imaging.
	•	Electron Beam Shaping: Advances in aberration correction and phase contrast techniques in electron microscopy continue to improve resolution.
	•	Plasmonic Lenses: These could focus light beyond the diffraction limit by manipulating surface plasmons, potentially improving optical microscopy.

For now, the highest practical resolution is achieved by advanced electron and scanning probe microscopes, but future breakthroughs in quantum optics and nanophotonics may push limits even further.

Author: @Richard-bq3ni
Content:
For scanning TEM (STEM) there is a corrector installed above the objective (where the sample sits). This is called the probe corrector. It reduces the abberations in the beam that scans the sample. Not only spherical abberations but other abberations as well like astigmatsm.
For TEM imaging there is a corrector below the objective, called the image corrector.
There is also chromatic abberation. This can be reduced by using an electron gun that emits electrons with an homegeneous energy, like having only one "colour" of "light".

Author: @Parents_of_Twins
Content: I worked with the STM and AFM in grad school. The first time I got a molecular resolution image I was so excited. By the time I finished up my research it was almost easy to get molecular resolution. We were using Pt/Ir tips hand cut with pliers and a gold beads annealed via hydrogen flame to create atomically flat facets several hundred microns in size. The tricky part is aligning the facet to be as close to perpendicular to the tip as possible. I never tried to get molecular resolution with our AFM setup. Our setup was far from new with everything being at least 10-15 years old at the time. It's sad how difficult it is to get funding for science and now a multi-billionaire controls our treasury so that should make it worse.

Author: @allenshepard7992
Content:
One correction - while TEM could not see atoms, even in 1980 and before they could see cells and parts of cells very clearly. Far better than light microscopy.  
Please do not get the impression that TEM did not work until 1997. It was a great medical advantage used to diagnose problems. 
Due to stains and if the sample had to be sliced, light microscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and TEM all gave different vires of the cells or sample. Hence each produced their slice of information.  
BTW the larger TEM are over a million volts and three stories tall, producing some X-ray radiation due to the electron velocity. They need to be tall because at higher speeds the electron spends less and less time in the magnetic field and is deflected less.

Author: @OmateYayami
Content:
Vision is some average over many individual interactions with matter. That's why it gets complicated when you zoom in. It's bound to get blurry due to physics, no matter what level you go. Eventually some physical bound will get hit. But it's fun to see different physical effects at different levels of resolution scales.

Notice that for more advanced methods presented here work with planes and pretty regular structures. Getting a 3D image of a molecule is way, way harder because you need to hold the sample in place and register more interactions, like literally an additional dimension of complexity.

The other problem is that better resolution usually means more energy so your sample needs to be resilient enough not to be destroyed. It's kinda exposure vs sharpness tradeoff known from classic photography but illuminating the object deteriorates it. It's fascinating engineering.
